record.title: Agima reports a single omni model planning with imagined visual outcomes in four simulated tasks
record.summary: An Oct. 19 preprint introduces Agima, which trains one 14B-parameter omni model (7B active) to propose actions, generate visual predictions of their outcomes, and plan from those imagined observations before acting. The authors report results across Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman and PushT. In a four-box Sokoban test with real feedback every five actions, the SFT model solves 40% of puzzles versus 2% for an action-only model fine-tuned from the same backbone. Replacing imagined observations with blank or stale frames sharply reduces success; oracle observations improve it, linking the reported gains to prediction content. Results are author-reported in simulated tasks; the research desk did not reproduce them, and the paper reports no inference FLOPs or latency.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The preprint reports that Agima, trained on two-box Sokoban, solves 40% of four-box puzzles when receiving real observations every five actions, versus 2% for a same-backbone action-only baseline.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across four simulated environments, the authors report that replacing imagined observations with blank or stale frames sharply reduces task success, while replacing them with ground-truth observations improves it.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper describes a two-stage method: supervised fine-tuning on interleaved action/image traces, followed by GRPO using task-success reward to adapt how the model compares imagined plans.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the reported planning gains or visual-prediction ablations was completed.
Transfer beyond simulated grids and tabletop PushT, and behavior under real sensor/model error, are unknown.
The paper reports action counts but not inference latency, FLOPs, energy or wall-clock costs for imagined rollouts.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported planning gains transfer beyond simple simulated settings, a single model that predicts visual action outcomes and plans over them could improve agents working with sparse feedback or irreversible actions. The implication is meaningful but bounded because the evidence is one paper-reported study in four simulated task families, without independent reproduction or measured inference cost.
limitations: All numerical performance results are reported by the paper authors; the research desk did not independently reproduce them.
The evaluation covers four simulated task families and selected held-out configurations, not physical robots or deployed environments.
The reported action-count reductions and success rates do not establish inference latency, FLOPs, monetary cost or energy savings.
The public repository lists checkpoints and dataset artifacts but excludes result tables and evaluation logs; no artifact was executed.
brief.summary: An Oct. 19 preprint introduces Agima, which trains one 14B-parameter omni model (7B active) to propose actions, generate visual predictions of their outcomes, and plan from those imagined observations before acting. The authors report results across Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman and PushT. In a four-box Sokoban test with real feedback every five actions, the SFT model solves 40% of puzzles versus 2% for an action-only model fine-tuned from the same backbone. Replacing imagined observations with blank or stale frames sharply reduces success; oracle observations improve it, linking the reported gains to prediction content. Results are author-reported in simulated tasks; the research desk did not reproduce them, and the paper reports no inference FLOPs or latency.

technical.claimed_result: At K=5 (five actions per real observation), the authors report 40% four-box Sokoban success after SFT on two-box puzzles versus 2% for an action-only same-backbone model. At K=5 they report gains over that baseline of 36 percentage points in Pacman, 17 in Maze2D, 38 in Sokoban and 17 in PushT. At K=infinity, performance and several gains shrink. In ablations, blank/stale predicted frames reduce success; oracle ground-truth frames improve success by 29–44 points in Pacman, Maze2D and PushT and 3 points in Sokoban.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv preprint documents the Agima method, four simulated task families and reported comparisons. the research desk did not reproduce the experiments or inspect runnable result logs.
technical.mechanism: A single BAGEL omni backbone is trained as both policy and visual world model. Supervised traces interleave actions with predicted future observations; linear rollouts, counterfactual branches and forward comparisons teach alternative planning patterns. GRPO then updates language planning traces from binary task-success reward while generated images remain context rather than receiving direct RL loss.
technical.novelty: The same omni model interleaves visual predictions and action planning, then uses task-reward RL to adapt how it considers imagined futures before execution.
technical.regime: Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman and PushT simulation. Training uses simpler settings, including two-box Sokoban; tests use harder or held-out task configurations. Appendix reports 100 episodes per set for key Sokoban deadlock/structural-fork evaluations. No real-world robot, deployed agent, inference FLOPs or latency evaluation is reported.
technical.reproducibility: A public code/artifact repository is linked, but its result tables and evaluation logs are not included. The README describes a five-episode quickstart; the research desk did not run the code or model.
technical.strongest_baseline: A separately fine-tuned action-only model from the same BAGEL backbone and task data, plus image-content ablations that replace imagined frames with blank, stale or oracle ground-truth observations. The model comparisons and outcomes are author-reported.

brief.title: Agima reports a single omni model planning with imagined visual outcomes in four simulated tasks
brief.why_it_matters: The work tests a practical planning design for environments where actions are costly or irreversible: one multimodal model predicts what actions will look like, then uses those predictions to choose what to do. If the reported gains generalize, learned visual imagination could help agents act with less frequent real feedback. The evidence remains bounded to four simulated task families and does not establish real-world robotics, production reliability, or compute savings.
